newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexican banker killed in botched robbery - police.
newsitem.headline: Mexican banker killed in botched robbery - police.

text.p: More evidence suggests that last weekend's murder of Finance Minister Guillermo Ortiz's brother was a botched robbery and not politically motivated, Mexican police said on Tuesday.

Police said Alejandro Ortiz Martinez, a 55-year-old bank official, was killed on Saturday after he tried to pull a gun on two would-be robbers who accosted him as he sat in his Mercedes Benz in an upscale neighborhood of Mexico City.
Based on a reconstruction of the murder, police said that after Ortiz reached for a gun under his seat, one of the criminals shot him twice in the head, took his gun and fled.
"This reaffirms our hypothesis that it was an attempted robbery," Luis Roberto Gutierrez Flores, director of Mexico City's judicial police department, told Reuters.
"The criminals approach, he reaches for his gun and the event turns violent."
After the attack, police found a magazine containing 13 .380 mm bullets belonging to Ortiz's gun under the car seat, the Mexico City attorney general's office said in a statement.

The statement also said two 9 mm cartridges in the car were fired by a pistol belonging to one of the robbers. Earlier in the day, police officials said they thought the robbers may have used Ortiz's own gun against him.
Family members said Ortiz always carried a gun for protection, and had reportedly used it just weeks earlier to defend himself from a similar attack.

Many ordinary Mexicans, soured by high-profile political killings in the past few years, suspect the murder was more than a simple robbery, prompted by his brother's Cabinet post or his own position at a leading Mexican bank.
The culprits apparently had time to smoke a few cigarettes before the crime, suggesting they may have staked out Ortiz.

A Tuesday editorial in the influential Reforma newspaper said authorities were too hasty in discarding a political or revenge motive, considering the victim's relationship to the powerful finance minister.

But police said the two robbers, whose descriptions fit members of a well-known car-theft ring, were prowling for victims when they spotted Ortiz, who was waiting in his car outside his home for his wife as the men approached.
"It had nothing to do with who he was. It could have been any Pedro or Juan," Gutierrez said.
